title: NEOWISE 3.4 um data show no median infrared change in Gaia-alerted fadings of young stars, and the strong infrared response of accretion bursts in only 8% of brightenings (2014-2024)
abstract: Question: For young stellar object (YSO) events in the Gaia Science Alerts (2014-2025), does the 3.4 um (W1) flux follow the optical change, as an accretion burst that heats the inner disc requires, or does it stay within the small change that dust extinction allows (dW1/dG = 0.03 to 0.11 for R_V = 2.5 to 5.5)? Method: We matched NEOWISE visits (2014-2024) to Gaia alert photometry within 15 days for 857 YSO-related alerts and fitted dW1/dG with bootstrap intervals and a permutation test. A time-shuffled null gives the false-positive rate of each class. Results: 508 alerts are testable. Six of eight unsaturated bursts with a published accretion driver have a strong W1 response (0.46 to 1.11); the two spectroscopic extinction events do not (0.13, 0.15). Fadings (n = 217) have median dW1/dG = 0.000 (95%: -0.031 to 0.029), equal to the null: the occulter covers the star but not the W1-emitting disc. 17% of fadings become brighter at 3.4 um (null 6%, p = 1e-8), as inner-rim shading predicts. Only 8.2% of brightenings (24 of 291; null 0.13%) have a strong W1 response, and brightenings above 1 mag have median slope 0.06 to 0.07, so most large Gaia-alerted YSO brightenings do not show inner-disc heating. Eleven strong-response brightenings with disc colours have no published driver in our control list and are accretion-burst candidates. Three 'YSO candidate' brightenings (Gaia19eyy, Gaia23cvk, Gaia23dmc) are B-type stars in Gaia DR3 without warm dust and with W1 changes larger than G; they are probably classical Be stars. Strict and relaxed contamination flags and 3, 7 and 15 day windows give the same result. Limitations: NEOWISE samples every six months; 349 alerts are untestable or saturated; the control set is small; a low slope does not prove extinction; no new spectra.
